short: A weakness in software, hardware or a process that an attacker could use to do something they shouldn't.
Code or a technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability. 'Exploited in the wild' means real attackers are using it, not just researchers.
A software update that fixes a bug or vulnerability. Most attacks use flaws that already have a patch nobody installed.
A temporary way to reduce risk (turning off a feature, blocking a port) when a full patch isn't available or can't be installed yet.
The second Tuesday of each month, when Microsoft (and others such as Adobe and SAP) release their security updates together.
A vulnerability attackers are using before the vendor has a fix. The vendor has had 'zero days' to patch it.
A vulnerability that already has a public patch. Attackers race to exploit it on systems that haven't updated yet.
Example code showing a vulnerability really works. A public PoC often triggers a wave of real attacks within days.
Several vulnerabilities used one after another, e.g. one to get in and a second to gain admin rights. Each bug alone might look minor.
The attacker can run their own commands on a system over the network. This is usually the worst outcome a bug can have, since it often means full takeover.
The attack works without logging in. Anyone who can reach the system over the network can try it, which makes the bug far more dangerous.
A bug that lets someone skip the login check entirely and act as a legitimate (often admin) user.
Going from limited access to more powerful access, like from normal user to administrator or root. Usually the second step after getting in.
Tricking a server into making web requests for the attacker, often to internal systems or cloud credential services it can reach but outsiders can't.
Getting a website to run the attacker's JavaScript in other visitors' browsers, letting them act as those users.
Sneaking database commands into input fields so the site's database runs them, often to dump or change data.
Using ../ tricks in file names to read or write files outside the folder an app is supposed to use.
Bugs where a program writes to or uses memory it shouldn't. Skilled attackers turn them into running their own code. Common in browsers and operating systems written in C/C++.
An app rebuilds objects from data it received, and crafted data makes it run attacker code during that process.
An attack that needs no action from the victim, e.g. just receiving a message triggers it. Often used by commercial spyware.
Crashing or overloading a system so legitimate users can't use it. A DDoS uses many machines at once.
Distributed denial of service: flooding a target with traffic from thousands of hijacked devices until it falls over.
Any software built to do harm: steal data, spy, encrypt files, or give an attacker control.
Malware that encrypts files and demands payment for the key, usually after stealing a copy to threaten a leak.
Ransomware developers rent their tools to 'affiliates' who carry out the break-ins, and the two split the ransom. It's why one gang name can appear in very different attacks.
Encrypting a victim's files and threatening to publish stolen data on a 'leak site'. Even good backups don't solve the second threat.
Stealing data and demanding money not to leak or sell it, sometimes without encrypting anything at all.
Malware that destroys data permanently. Sometimes disguised as ransomware, but there's no way to get files back. Often used in wartime cyberattacks.
Malware that grabs saved passwords, browser cookies, crypto wallets and files, then sends them to the attacker. Stolen cookies can let them skip MFA.
Small malware whose only job is to sneak onto a machine and download the real payload (a stealer, RAT or ransomware).
Malware that gives an attacker remote control of the infected computer: files, keyboard, screen, sometimes camera and microphone.
Malware disguised as something legitimate, like a fake app, a cracked game or a booby-trapped installer.
A hidden way into a system that skips normal security, planted by attackers so they can come back later.
A small script uploaded to a hacked web server that lets the attacker run commands through a browser. A classic sign of server compromise.
Malware that hides deep in the operating system (or starts before it boots) to stay invisible to security tools.
A network of hacked devices (PCs, routers, cameras) controlled together. Used for DDoS, spam or hiding attackers' traffic.
Malware that spreads to other systems by itself, without anyone clicking anything.
Software that secretly monitors someone. Commercial spyware like Pegasus is sold to governments and has been used against journalists and activists.
Malware that records everything you type, including passwords.
Malware that secretly uses a victim's computing power to mine cryptocurrency for the attacker.
A scam site or script that tricks crypto users into approving a transaction that empties their wallet.
The attacker's server that infected machines check in with for instructions. Finding and blocking C2 traffic is a key defence.
The part of an attack that does the damage, like the ransomware or backdoor delivered once the attacker gets in.
A social engineering trick: a fake error or 'prove you're human' page tells you to copy a command and paste it into Windows Run or a terminal. Doing so installs malware.
Fake messages that trick people into clicking, opening files, giving passwords or sending money.
Phishing tailored to a specific person using details about them, which makes it far more convincing than mass spam.
Scammers pose as a boss, supplier or colleague by email to get staff to pay fake invoices or change bank details. Causes bigger losses than ransomware.
Phishing by phone call (vishing) or text message (smishing). Fake IT help desk calls are a favourite way into companies.
Manipulating people rather than technology: using trust, urgency or authority to get them to hand over access.
A fake login page that sits between you and the real site, passing everything through, including your MFA code, and stealing your session.
Trying usernames and passwords leaked from one site on many other sites, which works because people reuse passwords.
Guessing passwords at scale. Spraying tries a few common passwords against many accounts to avoid lockouts.
An attacker gains control of someone's account, using stolen passwords, session cookies or a SIM swap.
Stealing the token a site gives you after logging in. With it, the attacker is already logged in, with no password or MFA needed.
Tricking a mobile carrier into moving your phone number to the attacker's SIM, so your SMS codes go to them.
Needing a second proof (a code, an app prompt, a security key) as well as a password. It blocks most account takeovers, but some types can be phished.
Spamming someone with login approval prompts until they tap 'Approve' just to make them stop.
A login method that uses cryptography instead of a password. It only works on the genuine website, so it can't be phished.
One login that gives access to many apps (SAML and OAuth are the standards behind it). Convenient, but one compromised account unlocks everything.
Anything that proves who you are to a system: usernames and passwords, API keys, tokens or certificates.
A password for software. Keys accidentally left in public code are scanned for and abused within minutes.
A dedicated box (physical or virtual) that does one network job, such as a firewall, VPN gateway or load balancer. Hard to monitor and often internet-facing, which makes appliances a top target.
Equipment that sits between an organisation's network and the internet: firewalls, VPNs, routers. Attackers love them because they're exposed, powerful and rarely run security software.
Lets remote staff connect securely to the company network. A hacked VPN gateway hands attackers the front door, so these are among the most attacked products.
Controls which network traffic is allowed in or out. Ironically, bugs in firewalls themselves are a common way in.
A filter in front of a website that blocks common attacks like SQL injection. A safety net, not a fix for buggy code.
Security software on laptops and servers that watches behaviour and can isolate infected machines. XDR extends this across email, cloud and network; MDR is a managed service that runs it for you.
The system a security team uses to collect logs from everywhere, search them and raise alerts. SOAR automates the response steps.
Security Operations Center: the team that monitors for and responds to attacks, often 24/7. Where many cyber careers start.
Clues that an attack happened: malicious IP addresses, domains, file hashes. Advisories publish them so defenders can search their own logs.
Tactics, techniques and procedures: how an attacker operates. Harder for them to change than IP addresses, so detecting TTPs lasts longer than blocking IOCs.
A free, huge catalogue of real attacker techniques, used by defenders to check what they can and can't detect.
Research into who is attacking, how and why, turned into information defenders can act on.
Proactively searching your systems for attackers who slipped past alerts, assuming you're already breached.
The process of handling an attack: contain it, investigate, remove the attacker, recover and learn. DFIR adds digital forensics.
A security approach that never trusts a user or device just because it's 'inside' the network. Every request is verified.
Giving every person and program only the access they truly need, so a compromise does less damage.
Splitting a network into zones so an attacker who gets into one part can't reach everything. Air-gapped means not connected at all.
An isolated space where code runs without being able to touch the rest of the system. A 'sandbox escape' breaks out of it, often the second bug in a browser attack.
A programme that pays researchers for responsibly reporting vulnerabilities. Pwn2Own is a famous hacking contest with cash prizes.
Reporting a bug privately to the vendor and giving them time to fix it before going public. Usually 90 days.
Authorised attacks to find weaknesses before criminals do. Red teams play attacker; blue teams defend; purple teams combine both to improve detection.
Capture the Flag: hacking competitions where you solve security puzzles to find hidden 'flags'. A great, legal way to learn.
Software Bill of Materials: an ingredients list of every component inside a piece of software, so you can tell fast if you're affected by a new bug.
Products the vendor no longer updates. New vulnerabilities in them will never be patched, so the only fix is replacing them.
Compromising something many organisations trust (a vendor, update or open-source package) to reach all their customers at once.
Registering names one typo away from a real package or website (reqeusts vs requests) so mistakes deliver malware. Slopsquatting targets package names AI assistants make up.
Public libraries of open-source code packages (npm for JavaScript, PyPI for Python). Developers install from them constantly, so attackers upload malicious look-alikes.
Software whose code is public and free to reuse. Most modern apps are built mostly from open-source parts, often maintained by unpaid volunteers.
Automated systems that build, test and deploy code. They hold powerful secrets, which makes them a prized supply-chain target.
A self-spreading worm found in npm packages in 2025. It steals developers' tokens, then uses them to publish infected versions of their other packages.
Advanced persistent threat: a skilled, well-resourced hacking group, usually government-backed, that stays hidden in networks for long periods. Many have numbered names like APT28.
Hackers working for or on behalf of a government, usually for spying, sabotage or (for North Korea) stealing money.
Security-speak for whoever is behind an attack: a person, gang or government unit.
Hacking to steal secrets: government plans, research, trade secrets or communications. Quiet, long-term and usually state-backed.
Hackers driven by politics or a cause. Usually DDoS and defacements, though some state-linked groups pretend to be hacktivists.
Criminals who break into companies and sell that access to others, often ransomware gangs.
Using a system's own built-in tools (PowerShell, admin utilities) instead of malware, so the attacker blends in with normal IT activity.
Spreading from the first hacked machine to others in the network, hunting for admin accounts and valuable data.
Tricks attackers use to keep their access after reboots, password changes or patches, like scheduled tasks, new accounts and backdoors.
Secretly copying data out of a victim's network to the attacker.
When information is accessed or stolen by someone who shouldn't have it.
Bring your own vulnerable driver: attackers install a legitimate but buggy driver, then abuse it to switch off security tools.
Remote monitoring and management software that IT teams use to control computers. Attackers install the same legitimate tools to keep access without triggering antivirus.
Ways criminals clean stolen money: mules move it through their own bank accounts, and mixers blur cryptocurrency trails.
Websites reachable only through anonymity networks like Tor. Home to criminal forums, leak sites and marketplaces, and to whistle-blowers and privacy users too.
AI-generated fake video or audio of a real person. Used for fraud, like fake CEO video calls requesting payments.
Large language model: the kind of AI behind chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. It predicts text and can now write code and use tools.
An AI that can take actions (browse, run code, send email) rather than just chat. More useful, and a bigger risk if it's tricked.
Hiding instructions in content an AI reads (a web page, email or file) to make it do something its user never asked for.
For AI: tricking a model into ignoring its safety rules. For phones: removing the manufacturer's restrictions.
Model Context Protocol: a standard way to connect AI assistants to tools and data. A malicious or compromised MCP server can feed an AI harmful instructions.
Artificial intelligence. In security news, usually large language models used by attackers, by defenders, or as a new target in their own right.
Computing rented from providers like AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. You're still responsible for configuring it securely.
Software-as-a-service: apps you use in the browser and someone else hosts (Salesforce, Microsoft 365, Slack). Data theft from SaaS accounts is now a major attack trend.
A security setting left wrong, like a database open to the internet or a storage bucket set to public. Behind a huge share of breaches.
Amazon Web Services, the biggest cloud provider. S3 is its file storage. 'Leaky S3 buckets' are storage accidentally set to public.
Microsoft's cloud platform, tightly linked to Microsoft 365 and Entra ID accounts.
Identity and access management: the systems and rules deciding who can access what. In the cloud, IAM mistakes are a top cause of breaches.
Containers package an app with everything it needs; Kubernetes runs thousands of them. Exposed dashboards and APIs are common targets.
A hypervisor runs many virtual computers (VMs) on one physical server. Ransomware gangs target hypervisors to encrypt hundreds of servers in one go.
Application programming interface: how programs talk to each other. Poorly protected APIs leak data without anyone 'hacking' a login page.
The app programmers write code in. Malicious editor extensions can steal source code and keys from developers.
Command-line interface: controlling a computer by typing commands. PowerShell (Windows) and Bash (Linux) are favourites of admins and attackers alike.
A device's address on a network. Attack reports list malicious IPs so defenders can block them.
A numbered 'door' on a networked device for a specific service, e.g. 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH, 3389 for Remote Desktop.
The internet's phone book, turning names like example.com into IP addresses. Hijacking it can silently send users to fake sites.
The encryption that protects web traffic (the padlock in your browser). It protects the connection, not whether the site itself is honest.
A digital ID proving a website or program is genuine, issued by a certificate authority (CA). Rogue or stolen certificates let fakes look trusted.
Scrambling data so only someone with the key can read it. End-to-end encryption means even the service provider can't read your messages.
A one-way fingerprint of data. Used to store passwords safely and to identify malware files without sharing them.
Checks a receiving mail server runs to see whether an email really came from the domain it claims: SPF, DKIM and DMARC. (SMTP is the protocol that carries email.)
Windows Remote Desktop (port 3389). Exposed to the internet with weak passwords, it's one of ransomware's favourite doors.
Secure Shell: the standard encrypted way to log in to and manage Linux servers remotely (port 22).
Windows file-sharing protocol (port 445). WannaCry spread through a flaw in it.
The low-level software that starts a computer before the operating system. Malware here survives reinstalling Windows.
Malware spread by infected USB drives. Still effective against air-gapped industrial networks.
The computers that run physical things: factories, power grids, water plants, pipelines. Attacks here can cause real-world damage.
Supervisory control and data acquisition: software operators use to monitor and control industrial processes across a site or a whole grid. An HMI is the operator's screen.
Small rugged computers that directly control machinery (PLCs) or relay data from remote sites like substations (RTUs).
Internet of Things: everyday connected devices like cameras, routers and smart TVs. Often insecure and rarely updated.
Services society can't function without: energy, water, healthcare, transport, telecoms, finance. Attacks on them are treated as national security issues.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: the global ID system for security bugs, e.g. CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell).
A 0–10 score for how bad a vulnerability could be. 9.0+ is critical. It measures potential damage, not whether anyone is attacking.
Exploit Prediction Scoring System: the estimated chance a CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days.
CISA's list of vulnerabilities confirmed to be exploited in real attacks. If it's on KEV, patch it first.
Common Weakness Enumeration: categories of coding mistakes (SQL injection, buffer overflow) that cause vulnerabilities.
Common Security Advisory Framework: a machine-readable format for security advisories, so tools can check automatically whether you're affected.
Traffic Light Protocol: labels saying how widely threat information may be shared, from TLP:RED (named recipients only) to TLP:CLEAR (public).
An official notice from a vendor or agency describing a vulnerability or threat and what to do about it.
Laws controlling how organisations handle personal data. Europe's GDPR allows big fines for misuse or poor protection.
The US government's cyber defence agency. It publishes the KEV list and orders federal agencies to patch.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (part of GCHQ) advises organisations and responds to major incidents. Several other countries have an NCSC too.
Computer emergency response teams, national or company-level, that coordinate responses to incidents and vulnerabilities (e.g. JPCERT in Japan, CERT-UA in Ukraine).
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation leads investigations into major cybercrime. Its IC3 unit takes public reports of online fraud.
US and UK signals intelligence agencies. Both spy on foreign targets and also publish defensive guidance.
International police bodies that coordinate cross-border operations to take down botnets, ransomware gangs and criminal markets.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology writes widely used security frameworks and runs the NVD vulnerability database.
A major cyber security training organisation. Its Internet Storm Center (ISC) publishes daily analysis from working defenders.
A US non-profit that runs the CVE programme, the CWE list and the ATT&CK knowledge base.
Open Worldwide Application Security Project: a community best known for the OWASP Top 10 list of web app risks.
Chief Information Security Officer: the executive in charge of an organisation's security.
Microsoft names hacking groups after weather: Typhoon = China, Blizzard = Russia, Sandstorm = Iran, Sleet = North Korea, Tempest = financially motivated criminals.

China-linked state groups. Volt Typhoon pre-positions inside critical infrastructure, Salt Typhoon broke into telecom networks, and Silk Typhoon (formerly HAFNIUM) is known for mass exploitation of Microsoft Exchange.
Groups tied to Russian intelligence. APT28/Fancy Bear (GRU) does espionage and influence operations, APT29/Cozy Bear (SVR) did SolarWinds, and Sandworm attacks Ukraine's power grid.
North Korean state hackers who steal billions in cryptocurrency to fund the regime. North Korea also places fake remote IT workers inside Western companies.
Placeholder names for groups researchers haven't fully identified: UNC#### (Google Mandiant), TA### (Proofpoint), Storm-#### (Microsoft), UAC-#### (Ukraine's CERT-UA).
A loose group of mostly young English-speaking hackers famous for calling help desks to reset passwords. Hit MGM, Caesars and UK retailers like M&S.
A data-theft and extortion crew behind huge breaches, including mass theft from Salesforce and Snowflake customer accounts. Overlaps with Scattered Spider.
The ransomware brand names that dominate headlines. Gangs often rebrand after police takedowns, and affiliates hop between them.
SonicWall Secure Mobile Access: remote-access (SSL VPN) appliances that let employees connect to their company network from outside. SMA 100 is for small businesses, SMA 1000 for large enterprises.
more: Because they sit on the internet and guard the way into the network, bugs in them are quickly exploited.

short: A US maker of firewalls and remote-access appliances, used heavily by small and mid-sized businesses. Its devices are frequent targets for ransomware gangs.
One of the biggest firewall and VPN vendors. FortiGate firewalls are everywhere, so their vulnerabilities are prime targets for state hackers and ransomware gangs.
Maker of VPN (Connect Secure, formerly Pulse Secure) and device management products that have suffered repeated zero-day attacks.
NetScaler ADC and Gateway are appliances that manage and secure remote access to company apps. Bugs like 'CitrixBleed' let attackers steal live login sessions.
A leading firewall vendor. PAN-OS runs its firewalls; GlobalProtect is its VPN. Both are high-value targets.
The world's biggest networking company: routers, switches, firewalls (ASA/Firepower). Its gear underpins much of the internet, which makes it a target for state hackers.
Load balancers and application gateways that sit in front of big websites and apps. Exploited bugs can expose everything behind them.
Major maker of routers and firewalls used by internet providers and large organisations.
Virtualisation software (now owned by Broadcom) that runs many company servers. ESXi is the hypervisor and vCenter manages it. Ransomware gangs build special versions to encrypt ESXi.
Popular backup software. Attackers target backup servers first so victims can't recover without paying.
Microsoft's email server. On-premises Exchange servers were mass-hacked in 2021 (ProxyLogon), and old unpatched ones remain a target.
Microsoft's document and intranet platform. A 2025 zero-day chain in self-hosted SharePoint ('ToolShell') was exploited against hundreds of organisations.
The Windows system that manages users, passwords and permissions across a company network. Taking over a domain controller is like getting keys to every door.
Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) handles logins for Microsoft 365 apps like Outlook and Teams. A hijacked account gives access to email, files and chat.
Microsoft's operating system, the most widely targeted desktop platform.
Windows User Account Control: the 'Do you want to allow this app to make changes?' prompt. Malware tries to bypass it to gain admin rights silently.
A major identity provider: the login system many companies use for single sign-on to all their apps.
Cloud platforms holding huge amounts of customer data. Recent mass data thefts came from stolen logins and connected apps, not bugs in the platforms themselves.
Platforms where developers store and share code. Leaked secrets in repositories and poisoned projects are common attack routes.
WordPress runs a large share of all websites. Its thousands of third-party plugins are the usual weak spot, with constant bugs that bots scan for automatically.
Workplace tools for wikis (Confluence) and project tracking (Jira). Self-hosted servers have suffered critical, widely exploited bugs.
Automation servers that build and deploy software. A compromise can poison everything they ship.
Managed file transfer products move sensitive files between organisations. The Cl0p gang mass-exploited MOVEit, GoAnywhere and Cleo to steal data from thousands of victims.
Legitimate remote-support tools. Attackers abuse them for hands-on access, and bugs in them have been exploited against IT providers' customers.
Popular remote desktop software. Scammers and ransomware gangs install it to control victims' machines.
A Java logging library used almost everywhere. Its 2021 'Log4Shell' bug let attackers run code by getting an app to log a crafted message.
The open-source library that provides encryption for much of the internet. 2014's Heartbleed bug leaked secrets from its memory.
A foundation behind many open-source server projects, like the Apache web server, Tomcat and Struts. The Equifax breach came through an unpatched Struts bug.
The core of the Linux operating system, running most servers, Android phones and countless devices. Kernel bugs often let attackers become root.
Google's browser. Chromium is the open-source base that Edge, Brave and Opera share too. V8 is its JavaScript engine, a frequent zero-day target.
Apple's browser engine. Every iPhone browser has to use it, so a WebKit bug affects all of them.
Phone and computer operating systems. Updates often fix bugs already used by spyware, so install them promptly.
Big makers of industrial and power-grid equipment. Their security advisories cover gear that runs substations and factories, where patching needs careful planning.
A small device that stores cryptocurrency keys offline. The seed phrase is the master backup: anyone who has it owns the funds.

The companies and chatbots behind today's large language models. In security news they appear as tools attackers misuse, as defenders' helpers, and as targets of research into AI safety and prompt injection.
The US Department of Justice prosecutes cybercriminals and announces indictments, arrests and seizures of criminal infrastructure.
Continuously finding everything an organisation exposes to the internet (forgotten servers, test sites, open ports) before attackers do.
A database product from Progress Software that businesses use to store and search large amounts of documents and data. Flaws in it can expose that data or let attackers take control of the server.

Ahsay Cloud Backup Suite, server software that backup providers and businesses run to store customers' backups. Because it is reachable over the internet and holds copies of data, unpatched flaws in it are attractive to attackers.

An Amazon Web Services (AWS) service for building and running AI agents in the cloud. Agents run there may hold credentials and permissions, so weaknesses can let a malicious prompt reach sensitive cloud resources.
Short for the People's Republic of China. Security reports use 'PRC-linked' or 'PRC state-sponsored' to describe hacking groups believed to work for or on behalf of the Chinese government.
A member group where organisations in the same industry, such as healthcare or finance, share warnings and information about cyber threats so they can defend each other.
SAP's software platform that many large organisations use to run and connect their business applications. Because it holds sensitive business data, flaws in it are high-value targets for attackers.
A short code that works only once, sent by text or email or shown in an app, used as an extra login step on top of your password.
A programming language built into Microsoft Office and some other programs, used to write macros that automate tasks. Attackers often hide malicious VBA macros in documents to infect computers.
A Windows and Microsoft Edge feature that warns you before you open websites, downloads or apps known or suspected to be malicious.
Transmission Control Protocol: numbers and acknowledges data so it arrives complete and in order, resending anything lost.
User Datagram Protocol: sends data without a connection or acknowledgements. Fast, but lost data stays lost. Used by DNS, video calls and games.
How TCP opens a connection: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. Both sides agree starting numbers before any data flows.
Internet Control Message Protocol: the network's error and test messages, used by ping and traceroute.
A tool that lists each router on the path to a host, by sending probes that may cross one more router each time.
A device that connects different networks and passes each packet one hop closer to its destination, using IP addresses.
Connects devices on one local network and delivers each frame only to the port its destination MAC address is on.
The router a device sends traffic to when the destination isn't on its own network.
A slice of a network. The subnet mask says which part of an IP address is the network and which part is the device.
A number like 255.255.255.0 that marks how much of an IP address names the network.
Writing a network as an address and prefix length, like 192.168.1.0/24: the first 24 bits are the network.
A hardware address built into each network card, like 00:00:5e:00:53:24. It only matters on the local network.
Address Resolution Protocol: a device asks everyone nearby "who has this IP?" and the owner replies with its MAC address.
Answering ARP questions falsely, usually claiming to be the router, so a victim's traffic goes through the attacker.
Network Address Translation: a router swaps private addresses for its one public address, and only lets replies back in.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: hands devices an IP address, gateway and DNS server automatically when they join a network.
Time to live. For DNS, how long an answer may be cached. For packets, how many routers they may cross before being dropped.
The server that looks up names for you, asking other DNS servers in turn and caching the answers.
Signatures on DNS records, so resolvers can check an answer really came from the domain's owner.
A virtual LAN: one switch split into separate networks, so devices only hear broadcasts from their own VLAN.
A link between switches that carries several VLANs at once, each frame tagged with its VLAN number (802.1Q).
A message sent to every device on the local network, such as an ARP question. Routers don't pass broadcasts on.
One chunk of data on its way across a network, with addresses saying where it's from and where it's going.
Seven layers describing how networks work, from cables (layer 1) to applications (layer 7). Used to pinpoint where problems are.
Border Gateway Protocol: how networks across the internet tell each other which addresses they can reach.
Signed records of who owns which address ranges, so networks can reject false BGP announcements.
The machine itself. A service listening on 127.0.0.1 can only be reached by programs on the same machine.
Shares incoming requests across several servers, and stops sending to any that fail their health checks.
A single front door for many services: it receives every request and passes each to the right server inside.
A cloud firewall attached to servers. It only has allow rules: anything not listed is blocked.
A connection that stays open after one HTTP request, so the server can push updates as they happen.
The number at the start of a web server's reply: 200 OK, 404 Not Found, 401 not signed in, 500 server error.
A random value added to each password before hashing, so identical passwords get different hashes.
Hash functions built to be slow, so each password guess costs an attacker real time.
An old hash function, broken in 2017 (SHAttered). Replace with SHA-256 or stronger.
Readable data, before encryption or without it. Anything sent in plaintext can be read by whoever captures it.
An old remote login protocol that sends everything, passwords included, in plaintext. SSH replaced it.
The protocol mail apps use to read a mailbox on a server.
A Linux command that prints every line containing what you search for. The analyst's favourite tool for logs.
A Linux command that runs one command as an administrator (root), and logs that it did.
Linux commands that change who may read, write or run a file (chmod) and who owns it (chown).
A DDoS trick: small requests "from" the victim make servers send them much bigger replies.
Changing a malicious domain's IP addresses every few minutes, using short DNS TTLs, to dodge blocklists.

Sender Policy Framework: a domain publishes a list of servers allowed to send its email. A receiving server checks the sender is on it. Results: pass, fail, softfail (probably not allowed) or none (no list).
DomainKeys Identified Mail: the sending server signs each email, and the receiver checks the signature with the domain's public key. Pass means it really came from that domain, unchanged.
Checks that the domain in the From line matches what SPF or DKIM proved, and says what to do if not: nothing (none), send to junk (quarantine) or refuse it (reject).
Faking where something comes from, such as an email's From address or a packet's source IP. The From line is just text the sender types.
An email header that sends replies somewhere other than the From address. A different Reply-To is a common phishing trick.
An email header showing where bounced mail goes. It usually reveals the real sending domain, which SPF checks.
The hidden lines at the top of an email recording who sent it, the servers it passed through and the checks it passed. In most mail apps: Show original.
An automatic action on incoming mail, like moving or deleting it. Attackers who take over a mailbox add rules that hide replies, so the real owner doesn't notice.
An MFA prompt that shows a number on the sign-in screen which you type into the app. You can't approve a sign-in you didn't start, which stops MFA fatigue.
The system of certificate authorities, certificates and trust stores that lets you trust a stranger's public key.
What you send a certificate authority to ask for a certificate: your public key and name. The private key stays with you.
Ways to check a certificate hasn't been cancelled early: a CRL is the CA's full list of revoked certificates; OCSP asks about one.
Watches network or host activity for attacks. An IDS alerts; an IPS sits in the path and can also block.
What a control does: prevent, deter, detect, correct, direct, or compensate when the usual control can't be used.
